facts.statement: The genus Purussaurus was first described by Rodrigues in 1892.
facts.quote: authority: Rodrigues, 1892

facts.statement: The type species, P. brasiliensis, was described by Barbosa-Rodrigues in 1892.
facts.quote: subdivision: * †P. brasiliensis (type species) Barbosa-Rodrigues, 1892

facts.statement: The species P. neivensis was originally classified as Dinosuchus neivensis by Langston in 1965.
facts.quote: synonyms: * Dinosuchus neivensis Langston, 1965

facts.statement: Purussaurus lived in the Americas during the Miocene epoch, specifically from the Friasian to the Huayquerian stages.
facts.quote: Purussaurus is a genus of extinct giant caimans that lived in the Americas during the Miocene epoch, from the Friasian to the Huayquerian in the SALMA classification.

facts.statement: Fossils of Purussaurus have been found in the Brazilian and Peruvian Amazon, Argentina, Colombia, Panama, and northern Venezuela.
facts.quote: It is known from skull material found in the Brazilian and Peruvian Amazon, Argentina, Colombian Villavieja Formation, Panamanian Culebra Formation, Urumaco, and Socorro Formations of northern Venezuela.

facts.statement: The largest known skull of P. brasiliensis measures up to 1.4 meters in length from the snout tip to the quadrates.
facts.quote: One of the largest known skull specimen (UFAC 1403) of the type species, P. brasiliensis, is measured up to 1.4 m in maximal skull length from the tip of the snout to the quadrates.

facts.statement: A 2015 study estimated the bite force of Purussaurus at around 69,000 Newtons, or approximately 7 metric tons-force.
facts.quote: Bite force has been estimated to be around 69,000 N (around 7 metric tons-force) in 2015

facts.statement: Purussaurus was an apex predator capable of hunting a wide range of prey due to its large size and strength.
facts.quote: The large size and estimated strength of this animal appears to have allowed it to include a wide range of prey in its diet, making it an apex predator in its ecosystem.

facts.statement: Adult Purussaurus preyed on large vertebrates like xenarthrans, notoungulates, and giant turtles, facing little competition from smaller carnivores.
facts.quote: As an adult, it would have preyed upon large to very large vertebrates such as the xenarthrans, notoungulates, and giant turtles present, with no real competition from sympatric, smaller, carnivores.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that Purussaurus's large size may have made it vulnerable to environmental changes, favoring smaller, more resilient species.
facts.quote: Researchers have proposed that the large size of Purussaurus, though offering many advantages, may also have led to its vulnerability.

facts.statement: Purussaurus teeth were consistently around 50 mm long and curved slightly backwards across all three species.
facts.quote: The teeth vary between the three species of Purussaurus, but are always around 50 mm (2 in) long and curve slightly backwards.

facts.statement: Ridges on Purussaurus teeth indicate it hunted large vertebrates by puncturing and holding flesh.
facts.quote: This indicates that Purussaurus hunted large vertebrates, as these ridges are used for puncturing and holding onto flesh.

facts.statement: Purussaurus teeth were taller and more pointed at the front, while being lower and more rounded at the back.
facts.quote: Teeth at the anterior are taller and more pointed, whereas those at the posterior are lower and more rounded.

facts.statement: Biomechanical models indicate Purussaurus could perform the 'death roll' maneuver to subdue and dismember prey.
facts.quote: Analysis of a biomechanical model of the skull of Purussaurus indicated that it was capable of performing the "death roll" maneuver used by extant crocodilians to subdue and dismember their prey.

facts.statement: Purussaurus had all sense organs at the top of its head, indicating it was an ambush predator similar to modern caimans.
facts.quote: All sense organs (eyes, ears, nostrils) were at the very top of the head, indicating that Purussaurus was an ambush predator like many modern caimans.

facts.statement: Purussaurus likely ate Stupendemys turtles, various crocodilians, birds, and mammals including sloths, bats, capybara-like rodents up to 700 kg, primates, and river dolphins.
facts.quote: The diet of Purussaurus likely included the extinct turtle Stupendemys, crocodilians including Charactosuchus, Gryposuchus, and Mourasuchus, Anhinga birds, and mammals including: sloths, bats, rodents related to the modern capybara (Josephoartigasia) weighing up to 700 kg (1540 lb), the primate Stirtonia, and river dolphins.

facts.statement: Bite marks on a phorusrhacid tibia suggest it may have been killed by a young Purussaurus, though whether this was scavenging or active predation is debated.
facts.quote: Bite marks on the tibia of a phorusrhacid from this locality are consistent with a caimanine, possibly a young individual of Purussaurus, though whether this represents scavenging or active predation is unclear.

facts.statement: New Purussaurus fossils were found in the Peruvian Amazon in 2005 by the Franco-Peruvian Fitzcarrald expedition.
facts.quote: During the summer of 2005, the Franco-Peruvian Fitzcarrald expedition found new fossils of Purussaurus in the Peruvian Amazon (600 km from Lima).

facts.statement: The name Purussaurus combines the Purus River where fossils were found and the Greek word for 'reptile' or 'lizard'.
facts.quote: The genus was named for the Purus River, where its fossils were first found, and the Greek word σαύρος (sauros) meaning "reptile" or "lizard".

facts.statement: Purussaurus is classified within the family Alligatoridae.
facts.quote: familia: Alligatoridae

facts.statement: Purussaurus belongs to the subfamily Caimaninae.
facts.quote: subfamilia: Caimaninae

facts.statement: Purussaurus lived in South America between 16 and 5.3 million years ago during the Miocene period.
facts.quote: Se trata de un caimán gigante que vivió en Suramérica, entre 16 a 5,3 millones de años, en el período Mioceno.

facts.statement: Some paleontologists estimate the full body length of P. brasiliensis was between 11 and 13 meters, making Purussaurus one of the largest known crocodiles.
facts.quote: El cráneo de la especie tipo, P. brasiliensis tiene una longitud máxima de 1,4 metros, por lo que algunos paleontólogos estiman que el cuerpo entero debió medir entre 11 y 13 m, aunque podía ser incluso mayor, convirtiendo al Purussaurus en uno de los mayores cocodrilos que se conozcan.

facts.statement: Purussaurus has two direct parent taxa in its classification hierarchy.
facts.quote: display_parents: 2

facts.statement: P. neivensis has been estimated to be 6.5 to 9 meters long and weigh 2 tonnes.
facts.quote: P. neivensis size has been estimated at 6.5-9 m (21-30 ft) in length and 2 tonnes in weight.

facts.statement: A 2022 study estimated P. brasiliensis lengths between 7.6-10 meters and masses between 2-6.3 metric tonnes depending on the method used.
facts.quote: A 2022 study also suggested a smaller size estimate, with an estimated length of 7.6 - 9.3 m and mass of 2 - 6.3 MT using a phylogenetic approach, and an estimated length of 9.3 - 10 m and mass of 3.95 - 5 MT using a non-phylogenetic approach.

facts.statement: Some studies suggest Purussaurus may have been heavier than Sarcosuchus or Deinosuchus due to its broader snout requiring a stronger neck.
facts.quote: One study also indicates that Purussaurus may have been heavier than either Sarcosuchus or Deinosuchus, as it had a much broader, shorter snout, which would require a thicker, stronger neck to support the larger head.

facts.statement: Purussaurus lived in environments including rivers, floodplains, and lakes.
facts.quote: Rivers, floodplains, and lake environments were present.

facts.statement: The environment of P. mirandai is described as tropical and coastal.
facts.quote: Its environment is described as tropical and coastal.

facts.statement: Three other extinct crocodyliforms, Sarcosuchus, Deinosuchus, and Rhamphosuchus, had body sizes similar to Purussaurus.
facts.quote: Three other extinct crocodyliformes, Sarcosuchus, Deinosuchus, and Rhamphosuchus, had similar body sizes.

facts.statement: Some estimates suggest P. brasiliensis might be the largest crocodyliform to have ever existed.
